articles.title: The New Forever Wars
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
DAFNA H. RAND is a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. She has served as Assistant Secretary of State for Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor and as Director of Foreign Assistance at the U.S. Department of State.
As the United States’ quagmire in Iran makes clear, wars are almost always much harder to stop than they are to start. Over the past 80 years, less than 20 percent of the roughly 300 wars tracked by the Uppsala Conflict Data Program ended in a clear victory by one side. A slightly smaller percentage ended in negotiated settlement; more than 60 percent had no formal ending. And the longer a conflict continues, the harder it becomes to broker a settlement. In wars fought between 1945 and 1989, another study found, mediation succeeded 37 percent of the time when it began within the first one to three months of fighting but only 19 percent of the time when negotiations began a year or more into a war.
The United States’ two-decade war in Afghanistan and decade-plus fighting wars in Iraq were no exception. In the wake of those conflicts, Washington has tried to avoid getting ensnared in so-called endless wars by avoiding deploying boots on the ground. In some cases, that means the United States relies primarily on airpower, as it has in Iran—an approach that comes with its own military challenges. But in many others, instead of participating directly, the United States is equipping close allies to fight shared threats and joint adversaries. Between 2010 and 2025, Washington more than tripled its annual security assistance for allies, from $15 billion to $46 billion, and increased its intelligence support and arms sales.
The United States has backed several of its partners’ wars in recent years. In 2015, Washington began coordinating U.S. intelligence and military support for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen. Since 2022, it has supported Ukraine in its defense against Russia’s invasion. And the United States has aided Israel throughout the war in Gaza following Hamas’s attacks on October 7, 2023. In all three campaigns, Washington supplied or sold the overwhelming share of the military hardware, intelligence support, training, and diplomatic backing. Yet its efforts had mixed results. The United States’ support greatly enhanced the military prospects of allies, but in every case, Washington found itself unable to shape how these wars were fought, and more critically, when and how they might end.
Supporting an ally’s war effort is often in the United States’ interest. But if Washington wants to participate in conflicts from afar, it needs a better strategy for maintaining influence over the primary combatants. It needs to enter with a clear idea of the war’s aims and how to achieve them. It needs to secure its partner’s commitment to the same objectives, to be honest with that partner about how far U.S. backing will go, and to set up mechanisms to ensure that the partner’s military adheres to American standards of conduct in battle. Ultimately, continuing to support allies’ wars without a shared strategy and without clear conditions for aid will not deliver the United States the advantages it seeks. It will only lead to more tension with close allies and more conflicts that don’t end.
Together with my colleagues at the Brookings Institution, I spent the past year interviewing more than 30 senior American officials, reviewing hundreds of public statements and documents, and consulting foreign officials to put together a comprehensive picture of how Washington engaged its partners during recent conflicts abroad and how those American efforts were received. What we found was that the United States tends to encounter many of the same problems when it supports its allies’ wars, even when the specifics of each situation vary quite a lot.
At the start of a conflict, Washington has much more power to shape a partner’s decisions than it does later in the war. When allies come under attack, they feel stunned and insecure, and they tend to seek Washington’s support in the belief that they will need U.S. military power to win their fight. Yet the U.S. government consistently fails to use its leverage early on. By the time it tries to push its partners to change operational designs, adjust tactics to minimize civilian harm, or come to the negotiating table, its influence has already eroded.
This failure can partly be attributed to the enormous political and moral pressure Washington feels to offer unconditional support when a close ally is attacked, as Ukraine was in 2022 or Israel was in 2023. Demanding strategic concessions from a beleaguered ally can feel like a betrayal. But holding back defers crucial conversations about goals, methods, and the limits of American aid.
Consider Ukraine. A few months into the war, the Biden administration publicly tied Ukrainian battlefield gains in May 2022 to the objective of improving Ukraine’s negotiating position with Russia, implying that Washington might expect Kyiv to start discussing peace terms before it could regain all of its land. But it is not clear that Ukrainian leaders understood or accepted the American strategy. As one U.S. official recalled, “It’s not that we didn’t take the time to think through the mission’s objectives—we did.” But Washington “recognized from the start” that its objectives of ensuring that Ukraine remained a viable sovereign state, maintaining NATO unity, and avoiding a U.S.-Russian war “were perhaps not the same objectives Ukraine had.” As a result, U.S. officials felt reluctant to push Ukraine toward diplomatic negotiations, especially while the Ukrainian military was advancing and congressional support for providing security assistance remained high.
Hard conversations with allies were also missing in the early days of the conflicts in the Gaza Strip and Yemen. The United States did not demand in the weeks after October 7 that Israel develop a “day after” plan for governance in Gaza once the Israeli military had sufficiently degraded Hamas—or even agree on what degrading Hamas meant. Had it done so, Washington could have had much more influence over how Israel prosecuted the war, insisting that non-Hamas security and political forces be allowed to start operating in Gaza once Israeli forces had eliminated large numbers of Hamas leaders in certain areas. Instead, as the war went on, the gap widened between the United States’ aim to prepare for post-Hamas governance in Gaza and Israel’s aim to destroy Hamas and prepare for military reoccupation.
Similarly, at the outset of the conflict in Yemen in 2015, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates promised the Obama administration that it would be over in six weeks. U.S. officials did not insist on seeing its partners’ plans for negotiating with the Houthis, particularly how they would handle the Houthis’ demand for inclusion in Yemen’s government. Washington spent most of the first few years of the conflict ramping up its support for the Saudi-led coalition rather than pushing for negotiations that could address the war’s political roots. One exception was a brief window at the end of the Obama administration, but at that point the parties simply stalled until the Trump administration took office. The Biden administration was also able to broker a cease-fire that lasted until October 7, 2023, but the war subsequently resumed. The Houthis are now stronger than they have ever been.
U.S. public and political support for aiding a partner’s fight also diminishes over time. Some of this erosion is a result of general war fatigue (and fatigue with providing foreign assistance), but support can decline more quickly if Americans consider the partner’s conduct in war unjust. In Yemen, for instance, bipartisan congressional support for the Saudi-led coalition collapsed within a year of the conflict’s start. During that time, depending on the source of the tally, anywhere from 3,000 to 9,000 civilians were killed, and by most estimates, over 60 percent of these deaths—as well as significant destruction of civilian infrastructure such as roads and factories—could be directly attributed to air attacks the U.S. military was supporting. By 2016, senators from both parties were publicly questioning why the United States was supporting these airstrikes. In 2019, Congress passed a war powers resolution directing the president to prevent U.S. forces from providing any type of logistical support for the bombing campaign, including aerial refueling and intelligence sharing. (President Donald Trump vetoed it, and Congress did not override the veto.)
In Israel’s case, American political and public support started off extremely high but soon began to drop sharply. A Gallup poll in the fall of 2023 found that 50 percent of Americans approved of Israel’s military campaign and 45 percent disapproved; some polls found even higher levels of approval. Yet civilian casualties in Gaza and Israel’s destruction of infrastructure and restriction of humanitarian aid quickly raised concerns. The Biden administration was able to change Israel’s conduct only on limited occasions, and it focused most intensely on improving humanitarian conditions, not on trying to reduce the civilian harm of Israeli military operations. During the first weeks after the October 7 attacks, for instance, it persuaded Israel to reverse a decision to cut off Gaza’s water, electricity, and Internet access, and in April 2024, after Israeli forces killed humanitarian workers from the U.S. food relief organization World Central Kitchen, U.S. President Joe Biden angrily called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and secured a temporary lifting of Israel’s restrictions on humanitarian aid. It was not enough to halt the decline in American approval of Israel’s campaign in Gaza. According to Gallup polling, 55 percent of Americans disapproved of the military operations in the fall of 2024, and 60 percent disapproved a year later.
Support for Ukraine has followed a different pattern. The conduct of the Ukrainian military has never been seriously contested, and most Americans agree that Moscow is the aggressor and that Kyiv is fighting a just war with important geopolitical consequences. Even so, the protracted congressional debate over a supplemental funding bill from September 2023 through April 2024 showed how support can slip. After Trump, the Republican presidential candidate by March 2024, questioned the amount of aid being sent to Ukraine, many Republicans in Congress wavered, catching Biden administration officials off guard. But as one official put it, “Ukraine fatigue” had already set in across segments of the Republican Party—Trump had merely activated it.
In every conflict, U.S. policymakers have a short window of opportunity before domestic approval for supporting a foreign war begins to shrink. As public backing wanes, it becomes increasingly difficult to pass bills in Congress that provide an ally with security or economic aid. The president begins to face pressure from the electorate to display less public support for the ally, which harms Washington’s relationship with the partner it is trying to both assist and influence.
Another factor limiting the United States’ influence over the course of an ally’s war is the partner’s ability to withstand American pressure. Strong foreign leaders often use congressional relationships, public diplomacy, and media access to resist Washington’s demands. Netanyahu has a long history of employing such tactics and did so again during the Gaza war. In 2024, he launched a public relations campaign to criticize Biden for holding up weapons transfers to Israel—even though the only delay involved the shipment of 2,000-pound bombs that the Biden administration deemed too large to be used in a place as densely populated as Gaza. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has displayed similar skill. Zelensky’s direct appeals to Congress for specific weapons pressured the White House to approve these transfers in the first years of the war, as did his criticism of the Biden administration’s delays in delivering more advanced systems. Worried about feeding Zelensky’s narrative that Washington was not bold enough in its support, some American officials hesitated to push Kyiv toward negotiations or to apply pressure when the U.S. military disagreed with Ukraine’s operational plans.
By acting too timidly around its allies, Washington has at times missed opportunities to change their behavior. When the bill for supplemental aid to Ukraine faced headwinds in late 2023 and 2024, Biden might have seized on the occasion to speak frankly with Zelensky about the limits of American support and the urgency of exploring negotiations while public backing in the United States remained strong. The Biden administration could have sent more technical experts and midlevel diplomatic staff members to Israel to convey concern about Israel’s rules of engagement as early as late 2023, when it was clear that the two countries were not on the same page about Israel’s choice of targets, choice of weapons, and approach to its first two major offensives, in Gaza City and Khan Younis. Later efforts of this kind appeared to work, as when the Pentagon persuaded the Israeli military to use limited strikes that led to less immediate civilian harm during the May 2024 offensive in Rafah or when the U.S. secretaries of state and defense sent a letter in October 2024 insisting that Israel lower its impediments to the delivery of humanitarian aid. Had Washington used similar tactics sooner, it might have had greater success at protecting civilians, ensuring that humanitarian access remained open, and pushing Israel toward operational strategies that would have limited civilian harm and been more effective against Hamas.
Part of the problem, however, is the structure of the U.S. government itself. Maintaining a coherent strategy across a sprawling national security bureaucracy becomes more difficult over the course of a long conflict. The president and his senior advisers often have an endgame in mind when Washington decides to support a partner’s war effort, but the task of building that partner’s military capacity and translating lofty political goals into a diplomatic strategy falls to bureaucrats much further down the chain of command. If these people are not given direct access to a partner country, they are not able to impart the United States’ objectives or learn more about the partner’s aims through the day-to-day practices of training and advising. U.S. allies can thus get their requests for military aid filled from afar, avoiding the forms of contact that would give the United States influence over their operational strategies and political goals.
During the war in Ukraine, for example, officials at the U.S. European Command, the National Security Council, the Defense Department, and the State Department have focused primarily on giving Ukrainians what they need to win on the battlefield. Meanwhile, without a large American diplomatic and military presence inside Ukraine, Pentagon and White House officials were sometimes left in the dark about Kyiv’s strategic and tactical plans. And the United States itself did not begin to seriously deliberate the terms on which the war might end—especially the scope of the bilateral security guarantees Washington might provide Ukraine—until 2024. In part, this was because there were serious disagreements within the government about whether the United States should push Ukraine toward negotiations at all.
Ultimately, it is up to policymakers to make use of the bureaucratic expertise and legal tools available to them to put pressure on foreign partners. During the war in Gaza, midlevel experts in humanitarian law and operational planners raised objections to Israel’s conduct, but they generally were not given access to the small circle of senior U.S. officials that made sensitive decisions about policy toward Israel. Key decision-makers did not make sufficient use of the extensive expertise across the Defense Department to guide the Israeli military on how to make gains against Hamas while minimizing civilian harm in Gaza’s dense urban environments. And the Biden administration did not invoke the Leahy Laws, statutes that forbid the United States from helping foreign security units that violate human rights, or Section 620I of the Foreign Assistance Act, which bans security assistance to a partner blocking access to U.S. humanitarian aid, to pressure Israel. The administration therefore left on the table some of the tools that could have helped it compel its partner to behave differently in combat.
Washington’s failure to pull all the levers at its disposal may also have led to missed opportunities for peace. In 2024, for instance, the Biden administration delegated the task of getting Hamas to agree to a cease-fire and hostage release deal to its Arab allies rather than pressuring the group itself. It also largely avoided public criticism of the Israeli government when its partner rejected the same deal, in the belief that any American rebuke would harden Hamas’s position and make it more difficult to reach an agreement in the end. Netanyahu and Hamas’s leadership remained intransigent, and the war continued into 2025. The United States should never have felt the need to choose between pressuring its ally to end a war and pressuring its ally to improve its conduct during the war. Both are important and can be done at the same time.
The Trump administration did apply more pressure on Israel to agree to a cease-fire in October 2025, ending major combat. But its failure earlier that year to continue pressing Israel to allow access for humanitarian workers and supplies enabled near-famine conditions in parts of Gaza, and its more recent failure to press Israel for a workable postwar plan has allowed Israel to occupy up to 70 percent of Gaza without making any meaningful progress toward a stable political arrangement. Once again, not applying pressure meant the United States lost control.
In Ukraine, Washington may have waited too long to devise a strategy for ending the war. At first, many U.S. officials were so focused on ensuring that weapons deliveries to Kyiv would not trigger nuclear escalation that they lost sight of the need to put Ukraine in a strong negotiating position. Others were hesitant to press Ukraine to make a deal, uncertain that they could accurately judge the country’s military prospects after underestimating its ability to hold back a much larger, more powerful Russian army in the early weeks of the war. But some officials believe Kyiv could have negotiated a peace agreement in mid-2022 if Washington had pushed its ally harder to engage in negotiations after the success of its Kherson and Kharkiv counteroffensives. The conditions for decisive action were there: Congress still staunchly supported Ukraine, and Europe and the United States shared a strong commitment to the war effort and to NATO unity. Today, Ukraine’s recent military success may yet prove that trying to win on the battlefield, however long it takes, was the right strategy, but Washington is likely to have less influence over any negotiations than it would have had four years ago. The United States’ standing with its European allies has eroded substantially since Trump returned to office, and many of them will not want to see Washington, with its questionable support for NATO and European security, dictate the terms of peace.
If Washington wants a say in how and when allies’ wars are resolved, it needs to find ways to work more productively with them while they are fighting. The most important lesson is both the simplest and the most difficult: American policymakers must use their leverage at the beginning of a conflict rather than wait for an opportunity that may never come. They should demand that a partner agree to a joint strategic plan as a condition of U.S. support, however difficult it may be to reach a consensus on war aims, postwar plans, and benchmarks for success. To formalize this joint plan, one U.S. official we interviewed proposed requesting that allies sign a written agreement reviewed every three to six months that lays out the terms of American support and the mutual obligations of both parties.
Another key to success is conditioning American security assistance on a partner’s adherence to the laws of armed conflict. When the United States knows that it will likely have concerns about a partner’s conduct—as when a war involves urban combat or the partner is fighting a nonstate group, such as Hamas or the Houthis, that itself abuses the laws of war—Washington should establish mechanisms as early as possible to adjudicate potential violations of the terms it sets. A standing review committee made up of lawyers and military experts should be insulated from political pressures and empowered to approve or deny security assistance based on clear benchmarks, including a partner’s meeting U.S. standards for military accountability and humanitarian access as established by the Leahy Law and the Foreign Assistance Act. These expectations should be conveyed to American partners at the start of the war.
The United States must also negotiate with the adversaries its partners are fighting. This is not a betrayal of American allies, but an essential part of making a settlement possible. U.S. partners are almost never able to end a conflict unilaterally. Washington’s tendency to focus on influencing its partner’s decisions while delegating engagement with the adversary to intermediaries—such as Qatar in the case of Hamas—ensures that U.S. leaders lack a clear picture of what it will take to successfully negotiate an end to war.
Finally, it is essential that the United States minimize conflict and confusion among its own government branches, departments, and agencies. When partners receive conflicting signals from different American officials, it is easier for them to play one U.S. agency off another. They learn to shop for the message they prefer and ignore ones they dislike. All levels of the U.S. government should be communicating and following one coherent strategy, from the president down.
For the foreseeable future, the United States is likely to remain heavily involved in its allies’ conflicts. Some partners may resist U.S. guidance on how and when to wage war, how to observe the laws of armed conflict, and which political outcomes best serve their security and Washington’s. Others, having witnessed the frictions that have emerged between Washington and its allies in recent years, are already following Israel’s and Ukraine’s examples in building up their own defense industrial bases to reduce their dependence on U.S. assistance. Yet in the end, when U.S. allies are faced with the prospect of war, many of them will still turn to the United States for the first-class military equipment and security, intelligence, and diplomatic support no other partner can offer. It will be up to Washington to ensure that when it decides to support a partner at war, it does so with a clear understanding of what leverage the United States has and how it can best use that leverage to keep its partner on a path that leads to the war’s end, on the best possible terms.

articles.title: China’s Quiet Quest to Dominate Latin America
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
NATALIA COTE-MUÑOZ is Managing Partner and CEO of Vantage Point Strategies. During the Biden administration, she served in the U.S. State Department’s Office of Policy Planning and as Acting Deputy Special Representative for City and State Diplomacy.
For years, U.S. officials have fretted about Chinese megaprojects in Latin America. Successive administrations have, for example, sounded the alarm about Peru’s Chancay Port, which is controlled and operated by a Chinese shipping giant, and about the Chinese-built Coca Codo Sinclair Dam, in Ecuador. In response, Washington has issued diplomatic condemnations against Latin American officials, revoked visas, and even threatened to use force against the region’s governments.
It is easy to see why the United States is so worried about major infrastructure being built and operated by China. In the eyes of many U.S. officials, these projects are a way for Beijing to accumulate leverage over Latin American governments—a concern that Washington has voiced since 2017, when the first Trump administration’s National Security Strategy warned that China sought to “pull the region into its orbit through state-led investments and loans.”
But Washington is stressing about yesterday’s challenge. Beijing is no longer betting on multibillion-dollar megaprojects to improve its position in the Western Hemisphere. Instead, it is embedding itself in the region by fostering smaller, quieter endeavors, often at the municipal or provincial level. Chinese firms are developing lithium projects in multiple Argentine provinces. They operate every power distributor serving the Peruvian city of Lima. And they are providing gear to Latin American police officers in many municipalities across the region, as well as installing surveillance camera systems.
Individually, these actions might seem superficial. But in aggregate, they are making recipient states dependent on China. Beijing’s security provisions, for example, mean that plenty of Latin American cities and provinces now effectively rely on China for their law enforcement and emergency response infrastructure, and, in Lima’s case, electricity infrastructure. It is a dependence that many national politicians never intended and may not even have seen coming. They may not be aware of the potential risks associated with this level and type of dependence and may not be prepared to manage the potential fallout.
These endeavors are not unique to Latin America. China is engaged in similar efforts in other parts of the developing world, as well. They are, after all, much cheaper than many of its earlier initiatives—and more difficult to identify. Beijing, in other words, is pioneering a kind of statecraft that privileges quiet, subnational capture over big, flashy projects.
During much of the 2010s, Beijing poured billions of dollars into in Latin American infrastructure, such as ports, massive dams, and even a transcontinental railway meant to link Peru’s Pacific coast to Brazil’s Atlantic. (The railway was never constructed, but versions of it are still under discussion.) These investments came as part of China’s famous Belt and Road Initiative, in which it has spent enormous sums on megaprojects across the global South. In doing so, China hoped it could secure commodity supplies, open markets for Chinese firms, and then convert its economic weight into diplomatic alignment—including convincing countries that still recognized Taiwan to switch recognition to the mainland.
But starting in the early 2020s, China changed course, particularly in the Western Hemisphere. Big projects, it concluded, cost too much at a moment when the Chinese domestic economy was under strain, and drew too much geopolitical backlash. Instead, it opted to focus on what it calls “small but beautiful” endeavors. These are investments that do not have an imposing physical presence and are typically aimed at smaller national and subnational systems. Beijing itself applies this label narrowly: its 2025 white paper on Latin America reserves the term for small poverty-reduction projects. But the phrase is a useful lens for this newer kind of Chinese statecraft—one of bottom-up investments that compound into interdependence and leverage.
To see how important this model has become, simply follow the money—or at least the parts that can be counted. Traditional Belt and Road loans to the region have faded from nearly $25 billion in 2010 to an average of $1.3 billion a year. But judging by estimates that track deals firm by firm, Chinese companies still invested $8.5 billion in Latin America in 2024, down just a tenth from the year before—and that figure is likely an undercount. The difference is that this money now flows through commercial transactions rather than through sovereign loans from Beijing. Much of it manifests in Chinese firms acquiring existing assets, such as power distributors and mines rather than the Chinese government spending on new megaproject construction. Other times, it still manifests as new hardware, but of a much smaller kind, such as policing gear. Because these deals are for items that investment statistics do not usually capture—equipment sales, training programs, donations, and maintenance contracts are procurement, not investment—they attract less notice. They are sometimes shrouded in confidentiality clauses, and often surface only when a local journalist finds the contract.
The Chinese government is still involved in this ecosystem, including, sometimes, through top-down directives. But its role can be more oblique. It often subsidizes its firms at home, which then go on to sell their wares to Latin American governments at low costs. As such sales and contracts pile up, China comes to recognize that the accumulated deals are strategic assets. Eventually, Beijing folds various commercial projects within a country into formal cooperation agreements with that state’s government. For example, in Argentina’s lithium-rich Jujuy Province, a research exchange between the two countries’ geological agencies grew into an explicit state partnership focused on surveying the province’s salt flats. Eventually, a Chinese company took a majority stake in a local lithium project.
China has worked its way into all sorts of local systems to build up its influence. Chinese firms, for example, have provided thousands of electric buses across cities in South America—a necessary addition in one of the world’s most urbanized regions. Chinese-made trains carry commuters on all three of Buenos Aires’s main electric rail lines. And perhaps most notably, China has been involved in providing internal security assistance. Safety is a major political issue in Latin America, where the homicide rate is around 20 per 100,000—three times the global average. Cartel and gang violence, cargo theft, and ransomware attacks loom large for most citizens, and so politicians repeatedly promise more action. China has offered itself as an affordable supplier of policing equipment.
Recipient countries often start by acquiring rudimentary provisions—donated anti-riot gear and armored vehicles for Bolivia’s armed forces, donated motorcycles for Caribbean police—each deal meeting the needs of officials short on equipment and under pressure to be seen as stopping crime. Eventually, the relationship progresses to more sophisticated items. In April 2025, for example, Rio de Janeiro’s governor flew to China and signed deals with the Chinese surveillance technology companies Hikvision and Dahua for more than 27,000 body and vehicle cameras. In the Mexican city of Ciudad Juárez, just across the border from the U.S. city of El Paso, local officials bought 1,000 facial-recognition cameras from the same two vendors (both of which were then on the U.S. Federal Communication Commission’s prohibited list). By 2018, 62 percent of Argentina’s surveillance equipment imports came from China, compared with just five percent from the United States. Today, at least 35 Latin American cities use Chinese surveillance systems.
Once these deals are made, cooperation accelerates. Sometimes, it reaches the highest levels of government. Consider, for example, the development of ECU-911—Ecuador’s nationwide emergency response system. The project began in 2011, when Ecuador’s government contracted with CEIEC, a Chinese state-owned defense-electronics company, to create a surveillance network running on Huawei cameras. A $240 million China Development Bank loan financed the system, secured not by sovereign collateral but by an oil sales contract committing PetroEcuador, Ecuador’s state oil company, to ship 72,000 barrels a day to PetroChina over the system’s operating life. In time, the project eventually attracted high-level attention from Beijing. In 2016, Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited Ecuador, where he personally inaugurated a joint security laboratory at ECU-911’s headquarters. Beijing followed up by donating 10,000 AK-47s to the Ecuadorean armed forces. By early 2018, Chinese facial-recognition technology was in use at ECU-911 sites. And in 2024, Ecuador’s independent municipal and private cameras were routed into the network. What began as one contract became the backbone of Ecuador’s domestic security apparatus.
Finally, China has been training Latin America’s law enforcement officials. Argentine, Brazilian, Cuban, and Panamanian delegations have all studied at the China Criminal Investigation Police University in Shenyang. In September 2024, China’s public-security minister signed a training agreement with Nicaragua’s police director covering narcotics, cybercrime, and terrorism; previously, China had given Nicaragua equipment for riot control. The United States still trains more Latin American police officers than does Beijing. But unlike Washington’s courses, China’s are bundled with cameras, platforms, and judicial exchanges that make the rest of its architecture stick.
Most important for China, these initiatives attract relatively little attention. Most projects, after all, start small—a municipal equipment contract, a provincial memorandum, a maintenance agreement. They are, relatedly, relatively inexpensive for China. A camera contract, for example, costs a fraction of what a dam costs, in addition to earning little attention. As a result, a country’s national politicians may not even be aware that cities are steadily handing over more and more services to Chinese businesses. U.S. officials might not realize it, either. Beijing can thus make investment after investment almost undetected until, suddenly, it has built much of a state’s critical security infrastructure.
Once China’s interlocking systems are in place, they are difficult to remove. This is deliberate. Over the course of its engagement with Latin America’s fickle democracies, Beijing learned that it needed a strategy that outlasts political cycles, as this one can. Once a city’s law-enforcement infrastructure is mostly made in China, its police and prosecutors have studied in Shenyang, and its courts have signed a cooperation framework with Beijing—as Venezuela’s did in 2023—the relationship acquires institutional memory and interpersonal ties. By cutting deals with regional officials, for instance, China builds durable political relationships that can quickly grow more valuable, should these politicians win higher office.
Moving away from Chinese systems is also financially difficult for recipients. A Latin American municipality that has inked multiple contracts with China and wants to diversify could probably find affordable, non-Chinese contractors for specific needs, like anti-riot equipment. But it is hard to move off integrated systems. It is also hard to find alternative suppliers for slightly more sophisticated items. China, for example, builds the world’s most economical and widely adopted surveillance systems. In the countries where it sells them, Chinese companies often drive domestic competitors out of business, thanks to generous government subsidies. Chinese cameras are, in turn, often impossible to service without continued Chinese assistance because most camera designs that the country produces are proprietary. Replacing them is extremely expensive and difficult. That means that when the cameras break, cities have to seek assistance from Chinese businesses. There is a reason why a 2020 study was unable to locate a single government that adopted a Chinese surveillance and policing platform and then completely got rid of it. Governments were more likely to restrict specific features than to rip the systems out.
As a result, many Latin American countries are highly vulnerable to economic coercion. If a state takes a position contrary to Beijing’s interests, China can tighten the screws on it by withholding spare parts, software updates, and technicians, turning a commercial partnership into a tool of leverage. Even without coercion, depending on China has frustrated many regional politicians. Ecuador provides a case in point. ECU-911 never measurably reduced crime; in fact, homicides in Ecuador rose from about 1,000 in 2016 to over 4,800 in 2022. The system also proved fragile. By 2022, roughly 1,100 of its 6,500 cameras were offline. Today, it barely functions, and Ecuadorian officials have grown unhappy with it. But the country has no alternative, and replacing the current system with a new one would be prohibitively costly and inconvenient. As a result, ECU-911 limps on, leaving the country reliant on Beijing for help managing its faltering emergency response mechanism. The same lock-in has already played out in telecommunications. The 4G networks of three of Brazil’s four major carriers, for example, were built by and are still serviced by Huawei, which made it impossible for former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro to ban the company from 5G networks, despite his best efforts.
But for other officials, the trade is well worth it, given the lack of timely alternatives. In fact, many regional leaders actively seek out Chinese systems, which provide pragmatic solutions to their countries’ security and governance challenges. They also offer up solutions for regional politicians so quickly that it overwhelms more careful responses. Some Latin American states even make preemptive political concessions to China in the apparent hope of quickly acquiring its goods. In March 2023, for instance, Honduras broke off formal relations with Taiwan and established ties with Beijing. Three months later, it signed 17 cooperation agreements with China, including one for smart city work, and it expressed support for China’s Global Security Initiative (a framework designed to help contest the U.S.-led international order). Within a year, Honduras’s 911 system awarded an uncompetitive contract for a Chinese video-management system, and the country installed 3,500 Huawei-made cameras.
The result is a sovereignty question that is uncomfortably familiar to the region: What happens when local and national governments work against their own citizens for the benefit of foreign actors? Often, the answer is that the foreign interests win. When indigenous populations blockaded Argentina’s salt flats over the environmental impact of Chinese-backed lithium projects (and over not being consulted before the deal took effect), Jujuy’s governor fast-tracked a constitutional reform to ban road blockades. According to human rights groups, provincial police also assaulted and illegally detained protesters.
Beijing’s efforts in Latin America have created risks that no one is properly accounting for. By building governance systems on Chinese systems, the region is trading short-term affordability for dependence—and, with it, Chinese leverage over its decisions.
But for China, the results are clear. Beijing has gained new influence in Latin America. It now has standing relationships in its municipal, provincial, and national governments, including nearly 180 sister-city agreements with 17 Latin American countries. China’s strategy also has no single point of failure. It bypasses the high-visibility sectors, such as ports, where it is most exposed to pushback, and instead embeds itself in the everyday needs of mayors, governors, provincial agencies, and low-profile central government departments.
Little wonder, then, that China runs the same model in other regions. In the Pakistani city of Lahore, the Punjab Safe Cities Authority installed Huawei-built command centers and 10,000 surveillance cameras on an $84.7 million contract. Kenya’s surveillance system runs on Chinese technology. China’s Ministry of Public Security has signed policing or security agreements with some 74 countries—featuring more than 200 deals in all. It has verifiably trained more than 12,000 foreign officers since 2000. Even in the United States, China made subnational inroads—namely, by selling port cranes to local authorities and operators—for years before the federal government moved to stop it.
In Chinese statecraft, doctrine does not always precede action. It can also follow the country’s choices, legitimizing and scaling what began as experiments. China’s first two Latin America policy papers, in 2008 and 2016, treated regional security as a sidebar to deals on trade and Taiwan. But its most recent one, published in December 2025, made security cooperation a central component. It did this because Chinese contracts and programs focused on Latin American policing and security were already functioning.
Because China’s doctrine ratified practice, the United States has been caught behind. To this day, it remains focused on guarding against a Chinese playbook based on building big, noticeable assets—ports, 5G networks, space infrastructure—rather than Chinese deals with municipal procurement offices and police academies. If the United States is serious about curbing Chinese influence in its hemisphere, it needs to pivot. It must figure out how to supply these actors with durable, effective solutions to their problems. Otherwise, China will remain the partner of choice for many in Latin America.

articles.title: The Looming Nuclear Crisis in the Gulf
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
YOEL GUZANSKY is a Senior Researcher and Head of the Gulf Research Field at the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University and an Associate Fellow at the Middle East Institute.
Since its announcement on July 22, the U.S.-Saudi nuclear agreement has alarmed nonproliferation experts. The 30-year deal would open the way for U.S. companies to develop the kingdom’s nuclear infrastructure, but it could also allow Saudi Arabia to pursue nuclear enrichment on its own soil. Although the agreement is still under congressional review, it has already created fears that it will weaken the U.S. “gold standard”—the strict requirements Washington holds nuclear partners to—and thus encourage other Middle Eastern states to demand similar capabilities.
Adding to the uncertainties, U.S. President Donald Trump declared a day after the announcement that the terms of the deal were “totally subject” to Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel by joining the Abraham Accords and insisted that “there will be no enrichment.” Neither of these conditions was apparently in the original announcement. Meanwhile, reports of confidential side letters to the deal have raised additional questions. Without knowing their contents, it is impossible to assess the agreement’s true implications.
Regardless of what conditions are present, however, the deal makes one thing absolutely clear: the central question is no longer whether Saudi Arabia will advance along the nuclear path but how its pursuit of nuclear power can be managed without igniting a nuclear arms race. Saudi Arabia is already in the final stages of completing an Argentine-designed low-power research reactor, and it has reportedly received bids from China’s National Nuclear Corporation, France’s EDF, Russia’s Rosatom, and South Korea’s Korea Electric Power Corporation to build two nuclear power plants. Although the kingdom has deliberately delayed making a final decision on those bids while negotiating with the United States, Saudi officials are determined to go ahead with their nuclear program as soon as possible.
This need not end in crisis. Rather than helping Riyadh make enrichment a national project and allowing it to go it alone on nuclear power, the Trump administration has another, better option: the United States should build a regional uranium enrichment framework through the establishment of a regional nuclear fuel bank on Saudi soil. Not only would such a mechanism reduce the risk of proliferation; it would also offer significant geopolitical and economic advantages, both to the United States and to the region. If Washington fails to explore this alternative, it could find itself facilitating the emergence of multiple national enrichment programs across the Middle East, driving a regional nuclear competition that will be far more difficult to contain than it is to prevent.
Nuclear nonproliferation experts have reason to take Saudi intentions seriously. In 2018, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman warned that if Iran went nuclear, Saudi Arabia would follow suit. Then, in September 2025, Saudi Arabia entered a mutual defense agreement with nuclear-armed Pakistan. Although that agreement did not mention nuclear weapons, it has reinforced the strategic ambiguity surrounding the Pakistani-Saudi relationship and serves as a reminder that Riyadh has alternative security options should it lose confidence in the U.S. nuclear umbrella.
Moreover, the United States has appeared to soften its position on Saudi nuclearization over time. In earlier years, Washington insisted that Saudi Arabia permanently forgo enrichment. Under the Biden administration, however, the United States considered building a U.S.-owned and -operated enrichment plant on Saudi soil as part of a broader Saudi normalization deal with Israel. Although the negotiations were interrupted by the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks and never produced a final agreement, the Trump administration now seems to have gone further.
Along with opening the way to Saudi enrichment, the July agreement does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which grants the IAEA expanded inspection and verification powers to ensure that nuclear materials and activities remain exclusively peaceful. Given the lack of Saudi transparency on nuclear issues, the construction of an enrichment facility in the kingdom thus carries the risk that the facility could be nationalized or diverted for military use during a crisis.
As of now, the Trump agreement is better understood as a framework than a final settlement. It leaves unresolved the central question of Saudi enrichment and nonproliferation requirements, and it has already triggered a new political battle in Washington over the future of U.S. nonproliferation policy. As a result, the deal is unlikely to be implemented in its current form without further negotiations or congressional scrutiny.
To understand why the United States needs to consider a different arrangement with Saudi Arabia, it is crucial to recognize that the question of enrichment remains central to the negotiations. The evolution of the Trump administration’s public messaging illustrates this. Following Prince Mohammed’s November 2025 visit to Washington, Energy Secretary Chris Wright insisted that the agreement “is not about enrichment.” Yet the July 2026 framework appears to leave open the possibility of a future Saudi enrichment capability. Whether this reflects a substantive policy change or simply contradictory signals, it underscores the lack of clarity surrounding one of the agreement’s most consequential provisions.
For Riyadh, civilian nuclear power is not merely a response to future energy demands or a component of climate policy. It is part of what it sees as a broader argument about sovereignty, status, and strategic balance. These issues directly shape how Saudi Arabia defines its willingness to commit to the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty (NPT) regime. The central distinguishing feature of the Saudi model is its refusal to relinquish sensitive components of the nuclear fuel cycle—above all, uranium enrichment—to multinational ownership or control. The kingdom is insisting that enrichment remain a sovereign national capability rather than part of a multilateral, IAEA-supervised fuel-cycle arrangement. Saudi logic is thus rooted in keeping its nuclear options open and securing its future freedom of action.
At the same time, Riyadh’s parallel dialogues with other potential nuclear partners, including China, has resulted in years of inconclusive negotiations, regulatory ambiguity, and continued uncertainty over whether Saudi Arabia ultimately seeks a conventional civilian nuclear program or one that preserves sovereign control over the full nuclear fuel cycle. The Saudi demand for a U.S. agreement that recognizes its right to enrichment is therefore not merely a technical issue but also an expression of deeper tensions in its relationship with Washington—tensions between its U.S. security dependence and its aspirations for strategic autonomy as a hedge against Iran.
The United States thus faces a dilemma. On the one hand, granting tacit approval to Saudi enrichment capabilities could set off a wave of regional proliferation should other states demand the same “right.” The United Arab Emirates, for example, might consider itself no longer bound by its own previous commitments to the United States. If Saudi Arabia were to eventually decide to pursue a military nuclear capability, the civilian nuclear project under development today could provide a shortened pathway. On the other hand, Washington has a strong interest in preventing China from getting access to the Saudi nuclear domain.
Equally important, however, is comprehensive international supervision of all Saudi nuclear-related activities. The kingdom must be persuaded to accept the full scope of IAEA safeguards, including the intrusive inspections required by the Additional Protocol. None of this is guaranteed in the current framework of the U.S.-Saudi deal.
One way to satisfy Riyadh’s quest for nuclear power that avoids most of these risks is to establish a regional nuclear fuel bank on Saudi soil. Such a project could be led by the United States and would be owned and managed by the IAEA. It would be designed to serve all Middle Eastern states that are parties to the NPT, including Iran. There is already a successful example of such a facility; in Kazakhstan, a fuel bank controlled by the IAEA supplies low-enriched uranium for civilian use.
A regional fuel bank offers many advantages. For Saudi Arabia, hosting the bank on its own soil could bring it the international prestige it craves but in a multilateral framework. It would also curb the appetite of states such as Egypt, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates for independent nuclear development, thereby lowering the danger of a nuclear arms race in the Middle East. As the exclusive supplier of enriched uranium, the regional fuel bank would impose de facto limitations on their nuclear programs, yet by its existence, it would also lower their potential opposition to Saudi Arabia’s nuclear program.
At the same time, such a framework would deepen U.S. oversight of Saudi nuclear activities and help block potential Chinese penetration into the sector. IAEA ownership and supervision would also build international confidence in the peaceful nature of the program. And significant U.S. involvement in the construction and operation of the facility would provide Washington with sustained insight into Saudi nuclear activities, making deception more difficult.
Establishing a regional fuel bank would not reduce the threat from Iran itself, nor would it eliminate Saudi incentives to hedge if Iran eventually acquired nuclear weapons. But it would make it easier for Saudi Arabia to meet its civilian nuclear needs without developing a domestic enrichment capability, thereby making any future regional nuclear competition less likely. At the same time, guaranteed access to nuclear fuel under IAEA oversight would reduce the rationale for Saudi Arabia—and other regional states—to pursue domestic enrichment capabilities in response to Iran’s advancing nuclear program. In the long term, this framework could eventually provide a diplomatic model for addressing Iran’s own nuclear program, offering guaranteed access to reactor fuel under international auspices.
Such a project is not without risks. It could encourage states that might otherwise abstain from nuclear development to reconsider. Nevertheless, the drawbacks are relatively limited compared with the dangers posed by Saudi Arabia operating a fully autonomous nuclear fuel cycle, including a nationally controlled enrichment facility. Moreover, the volatile regional context underscores the need for innovative risk management. The Middle East is already experiencing a low-intensity nuclear competition, at least in its civilian dimension, and the challenge facing policymakers is how to slow and manage this trend. The real choice is not between enrichment and no enrichment but between a proliferation-prone national enrichment program and a multilateral, IAEA-supervised fuel-cycle arrangement that minimizes regional incentives for a nuclear arms race.
Today, the question is no longer whether Saudi Arabia will eventually be permitted to enrich uranium but under what conditions, under whose control, and with what implications for the global nonproliferation regime. As of now, the July framework seems unlikely to survive in its current form. Congress, for example, could insist on stronger nonproliferation conditions, such as an explicit prohibition on enrichment; the adoption of the IAEA Additional Protocol; or tighter safeguards. Saudi Arabia might well reject those additional conditions, particularly if they limit its sovereign control over the fuel cycle.
Trump’s declared requirement that Saudi Arabia also normalize relations with Israel could itself derail the agreement. In both Israel and the United States, there is little appetite to give Saudi Arabia sensitive nuclear capabilities without a major strategic payoff. But Riyadh may continue to insist that meaningful progress must be made on the Palestinian issue before any normalization can happen. Whatever the outcome, any relaxation of the traditional U.S. standard should be accompanied by equally strong nonproliferation safeguards.
A better way out of the current situation is to reframe enrichment not as a national right but as a regional, internationally controlled service. Such an approach would transform nuclear enrichment from a concession into a conditional reward. It would align American nonproliferation interests with Israeli security concerns and give Saudi Arabia a clear strategic choice: nuclear legitimacy and international status in exchange for transparency, restraint, and regional integration. If Saudi Arabia were to accept a regional fuel bank in lieu of a sovereign enrichment capability, that arrangement need not be conditioned on immediate normalization with Israel. Instead, it could become part of a broader, phased regional process in which progress on civilian nuclear cooperation, regional security, and normalization reinforce one another over time. In the larger strategic picture, nonproliferation is more important than normalization.
articles.summary: Overcoming the enrichment dilemma in the Saudi deal.

articles.title: The Ambiguity Spiral in Iran
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ERIK LIN-GREENBERG is an Associate Professor in the Department of Political Science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Ambiguity—vague language, mixed messaging, frequent policy shifts—has been a hallmark of the United States’ approach to the war in Iran. From almost the moment the conflict began, U.S. President Donald Trump has vacillated over its purpose, what risks he might be willing to take, and what the United States would consider victory. He has threatened to destroy Iranian civilization, then promptly signed a cease-fire agreement. He has floated the possibility of taking Kharg Island, the hub of Iran’s oil industry, only to quickly walk it back. And he has discussed imposing a 20 percent toll on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, only to declare that the waterway must be free to everyone.
In some cases, ambiguity can help countries settle wars. Leaders, for example, can leverage uncertainty to de-escalate a conflict or reach a stable peace agreement by letting both sides claim victory. If governments avoid drawing clear redlines, they can avoid pressure to escalate in response to attacks, creating space to cool tensions.
But Washington’s mixed messaging about the war in Iran has done more harm than good. Trump’s spectrum of threats, for example, prompted Tehran to see the war in existential terms and maximally fight back. The lack of clarity over the status of the Strait of Hormuz made the June memorandum of understanding negotiated by the two countries impossibly frail. To reach a more durable truce, the Trump administration needs to be clearer about its goals and more consistent in pursuing them. Otherwise, Iran and the United States will continue to get their wires crossed—and the next cease-fire could again collapse.
When coercing a rival, a government must decide how to convey intent, capabilities, and redlines. One option is to be clear: explicitly and consistently defining a goal, identifying consequences for noncompliance, and articulating what the other side can count on if demands are met. Such clarity can let a rival state know what is at stake and encourage it to limit its response. But too much of it can do the opposite. If the rival knows just how far it can go toward a threshold without triggering retaliation, it will often escalate all the way to that point.
The other option is to be vague. Yet this can also have mixed consequences. If a state does not know how its adversary will respond to a certain action, it might hold back for fear of triggering painful counterattacks. But too many mixed signals can throw off an opponent’s risk calculus, giving rise to misunderstandings that can produce or worsen a crisis.
This is what happened with the United States’ Operation Epic Fury—its military operation against Iran. Trump has variously said, at different times, that the goal of the campaign is to degrade Iran’s missile capabilities and navy, prevent the country from obtaining nuclear weapons, and end Iran’s support of its regional proxy network. On the first day of the conflict, he even suggested he wanted to dismantle the Islamic Republic. (On February 28, Trump encouraged Iranians to “take over” their government, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has carried out military strikes alongside Trump, echoed that sentiment.) Other Trump administration officials, meanwhile, avoided explicit mention of a political transformation for Iran, focusing on narrower military objectives.
For Iran, this mixed messaging was the opposite of reassuring. Uncertain of U.S. intentions, its officials assumed the worst—particularly given that airstrikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in the conflict’s opening hours. The country thus escalated massively, unleashing thousands of missiles and drones at infrastructure and U.S. military bases across the Middle East. If the United States had been clear from the outset that it was not gunning for regime change, Iran might have responded with more restraint and the conflict might have stayed more limited, as it had after U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iran in June 2025.
Ambiguity has not only ramped up the conflict. It has also undermined efforts at ending it. The June memorandum of understanding was meant to pause fighting, open the Strait of Hormuz, and start a 60-day period for further negotiations. But it failed, in part because of its unclear wording. The memorandum obliged Iran to “make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels.” The Americans interpreted this clause to mean that Iran would let all traffic through, as it did before the war. The Iranians, on the other hand, took it as a confirmation that they had authority over the waterway and only needed to open parts of it. (Iran wants shipping to pass through the part of the strait closest to its territory). At the end of June, Iran began shooting at commercial vessels for taking what it deemed to be unauthorized routes through the channel. As these attacks unfolded, Iran’s deputy foreign minister took to social media to announce that safe passage was “not guaranteed under vague arrangements.” The United States interpreted these strikes as violations of the cease-fire, so it responded by firing at Iran. A similar tit for tat played out in mid-July, resulting in the fighting that continues today.
Although all conflicts are confusing and chaotic to some degree—hence the term “fog of war”—the one in Iran seems particularly ambiguous. Much of this ambiguity stems not from a calculated strategy to leverage obscurity for military or political gain, but from Washington’s struggle to settle on a desired end state. Deliberate ambiguity increases uncertainty by keeping opponents guessing. But when a country is ambiguous about its direction because of internal indecision, it tends to routinely back down from threats only to reissue them, eroding its credibility instead of merely throwing off opponents.
Still, the Trump administration is not fully to blame for the United States’ ambiguous posture. There are factors outside its control that undercut the White House’s ability to send clear and credible signals to Iran. Weak domestic support for the war, for example, makes it harder to convincingly threaten Tehran. According to July polling by The Washington Post and Ipsos, 68 percent of Americans believe that the war is “not worth fighting.” Tehran is well aware of this fact, which functions as a caveat to all of Trump’s statements. Even when the president makes seemingly clear and direct threats, Iranian officials cannot be sure he will follow through, given his domestic political constraints. Iran, in turn, may feel emboldened to brush off the administration’s threats and demands.
The United States’ relationship with its partners in the region also clouds its messaging and invites escalation. American armed forces launched the war alongside Israel, which has different interests, redlines, and objectives. In April, for example, Washington and Tehran signed a two-week cease-fire to stop the fighting, but Israel’s obligations under the pact were unclear. The Iranians said the deal required Israel to halt attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon; Israel argued that operations in Lebanon fell outside the pact’s remit. Washington backed its ally, and Israel ramped up strikes on Hezbollah targets. Tehran in turn accused American leaders of “oath-breaking” and likely concluded that the United States was not a credible negotiating partner because it could not stop its regional ally. Iran retaliated with missile attacks on Israel weeks later.
Although ambiguity has been an escalatory force in the war with Iran, that does not mean it always worsens conflict. At times, it provides policymakers with room to maneuver, to downplay hostility, or to exaggerate their own accomplishments. Indeed, U.S. officials have, on occasion, leveraged ambiguity to achieve this very effect. Weeks after the April cease-fire was signed, Tehran launched drones and missiles at American warships in the Strait of Hormuz. This could easily have triggered a descent back into full-scale conflict. Yet because the exact terms of the April cease-fire were never publicly released, Trump was able to downplay the incident. The president told reporters that Iran had merely “trifled with us,” insisting the truce remained intact. When the United States launched retaliatory strikes, Trump soft-pedaled their significance, referring to them as “just a love tap.” Central Command similarly announced that it did “not seek escalation.” Iran appeared to accept that narrative and held off on more strikes.
Moreover, whether intentional or the result of incoherent policy, ambiguity can allow both Washington and Tehran to claim wins. For instance, because the Trump administration has offered a variety of aims for its war, it was able to claim it had successfully achieved several core objectives upon signing the June memorandum—destroying Iran’s missile capacity, degrading its navy, and limiting the reach of Tehran’s proxies—even though the military campaign had failed to compel Iran to change regimes or abandon its nuclear pursuits. Iranian leaders, for their part, could declare that they succeeded by virtue of staying in power, inflicting damage on U.S. and Gulf infrastructure, and demonstrating their chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz.
These mutual declarations of victory ultimately could not save the memorandum. But similar assertions have de-escalated past crises. When Iran launched a barrage of missiles and drones at Israel in April 2024, Israel highlighted its success at defending its territory before retaliating with precision strikes against Iranian military targets. Iran’s government and media glossed over the damage caused by Israeli attacks and focused public attention on the fact that it had directly struck Israel for the first time. The lack of a clear outcome meant both sides could claim success, averting escalation.
A deliberate degree of ambiguity could also help end this conflict. If American and Iranian leaders keep their redlines vague when dealing with low-level military interactions, they will create off-ramps. But on the whole, the best way for the United States to settle the war with Iran is to be clearer about its objectives. The goals of Iran’s regime are evident: to maintain its grip on power at home, deter future attacks from its enemies, keep control over the Strait of Hormuz, secure release of frozen funds, and gain relief from sanctions. If Washington can sharpen its demands and communicate them consistently, both sides will be better able to focus negotiations and develop more viable plans for implementation—leading to a more durable agreement.
articles.summary: How Trump’s lack of clarity leads to escalation.

articles.title: Why a Weaker Russia Keeps Fighting
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ALEXANDER GABUEV is Director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin.
ALEXANDRA PROKOPENKO is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin. She worked at Russia’s central bank until early 2022.
TATIANA STANOVAYA is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center and the Founder and CEO of the political analysis firm R.Politik.
At the end of June, Russian President Vladimir Putin gave an interview in which he declared, once again, that Russia would win its war against Ukraine. The Russian army, he said, was advancing along the roughly 800-mile frontline and occupying more Ukrainian land every day. Kyiv, by contrast, was flailing. He acknowledged that the Ukrainian drone strikes torching Russian oil refineries and other critical infrastructure deep behind the frontlines were “creating problems.” But Russians would adapt and persevere. “These terrorist attacks have no impact whatsoever on the situation,” he said.
If this were 20 months ago, Putin’s confidence would have been warranted. At the time, recently elected U.S. President Donald Trump was praising Moscow and criticizing Kyiv. Russian troops were making slow but steady gains on the battlefield. Putin could thus follow three strategies, as we argued in a March 2025 Foreign Affairs essay. Under Plan A, the Kremlin would work with the White House to make Kyiv accept a deal written in Moscow. Under Plan B, Putin would simply hold out until Trump pulled U.S. support for Ukraine, allowing Russian troops to roll to victory. Failing that, Putin could pivot to Plan C: continuing to fight and ultimately prevailing on the battlefield.
Today, however, Russia’s position has deteriorated. Plan A—winning over Trump—failed; Putin didn’t even mention the U.S. president in his recent interview. Plan B also went awry. Although the White House stopped providing Ukraine with many types of assistance, the United States has continued to supply vital intelligence to Kyiv and enforce sanctions against Russia. Meanwhile, Kyiv has been able to turn to its European backers to make up for the lost aid. In fact, Ukraine is now better positioned militarily than it was last year. Russia, by contrast, is losing more soldiers than it can recruit and stalling out on the battlefield. Its economy is facing increasing trouble. Thus, Plan C, in which Russia would win by outlasting Ukraine, is also not working.
But that does not mean Putin will change course. Russia’s problems are real, but the country is nonetheless capable of sustaining the conflict. Its economy remains functional enough, and it has the manpower and weaponry needed to keep battling. Moscow is also devising new ways to regain the initiative. The Kremlin’s insistence on continuing to fight will make life worse for Russians, and so there are elites in Moscow calling for a negotiated resolution. But there is no indication that Putin is listening. The war, then, is almost certain to drag on.
When Trump took office in 2025, the Kremlin believed it could achieve a diplomatic coup. During the 2024 campaign, Trump had pledged to end the war in Ukraine “within 24 hours.” Upon taking office, he moved to pressure Ukraine’s leaders to accede to some of Russia’s demands. In February 2025, he insisted that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky agree to an immediate cease-fire with Russia and insinuated that Kyiv was responsible for the war. When Zelensky refused, Trump temporarily suspended intelligence sharing and military aid to Ukraine. Vice President JD Vance delivered a speech at the 2025 Munich Security Conference in which he declared that the United States was pulling back from Europe. And in August 2025, Trump and Putin held an amiable summit in Alaska. Afterward, the U.S. president said, again, that Zelensky was the reason the conflict wasn’t finished.
The trajectory of the Russian economy and the dynamics of the battlefield further boosted Putin’s confidence. In 2024, Russia’s GDP grew by 4.3 percent, fueled by military production and domestic consumption. Inflation was high but manageable. The Russian armed forces were recruiting more men than they were losing, whereas the Ukrainian army was losing more soldiers than it was gaining. The creeping occupation of the Donbas was costing Russia tens of thousands of troops, but these losses were tolerated as the country continued to advance. In 2024, Putin captured around 1,600 square miles of Ukrainian territory. Russia was producing nearly as many drones as Ukraine and using them in increasingly creative ways. It was producing far more traditional weapons, such as artillery shells and missiles, than was Ukraine or its Western partners. From the Kremlin’s viewpoint, a Russian victory was inevitable.
But not for the first time, Putin’s complacency led to overconfidence. He continued to push for conditions that Trump either could not accept or could not deliver—including that Kyiv surrender parts of the Donbas it still controlled and sign away much of its sovereignty. Trump’s two main envoys to Moscow, his friend Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner, were amateurs in international diplomacy and proved unable to start a proper negotiating process. In Moscow, attitudes toward both men soured. Plan A failed.
For a time, Putin could still hope that Plan B, in which Trump would simply wash his hands of Ukraine, would succeed. In March 2025, Trump permanently stopped supplying Ukraine with free U.S. weapons, dealing a blow to Kyiv. By July 2025, he had zeroed out American financial assistance to the country. But smart diplomacy by Ukrainian officials and their European allies ultimately persuaded Trump to keep sharing intelligence with Kyiv and to continue selling weapons to Ukraine via a program paid for by Europe. The Europeans also stepped in to provide Ukraine with the financial assistance Washington had yanked, and they turned the continent into the secure rear of Ukraine’s defense industrial base—providing money, technology, and safe locations in EU territory for Ukraine to manufacture its own drones and missiles. At the same time, Trump grew frustrated with Putin over Russia’s failure to entertain any concessions. He kept existing sanctions against Russia in place and even blacklisted the Kremlin’s two largest oil companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, putting pressure on Putin’s war chest.
With the failure of Plans A and B, Putin proceeded to Plan C—winning the war on the battlefield. Yet this plan is beginning to falter, as well. The war effort itself is clearly floundering: in 2025, the Russian army captured more than 1,600 square miles of Ukrainian territory (at a tremendously high cost in terms of casualties), but in the first half of this year, it advanced, at most, around 250 square miles. That is, in part, because Ukraine has built additional lines of defense with fortifications and minefields. It is also because Ukrainians have been able to expand what analysts call the “kill zone,” or the area along the frontlines where Russian soldiers are almost immediately detected by Ukraine’s drones and then hit.
The result has been even greater Russian fatalities. Although public data is unavailable, according to the Carnegie Endowment military analyst Michael Kofman, the number of Russian soldiers killed each month has almost certainly risen dramatically over the last 18 months. Taken together, the number of Russian troops either killed or grievously wounded each month sits at roughly 30,000. Meanwhile, the number of troops who join each month has fallen to 27,000—the result of dwindling sign-up bonuses in some Russian regions and a growing awareness of the death count. Moscow’s ability to decisively breach the Ukrainian frontline is increasingly in doubt.
The Kremlin is facing other troubles, too. Ukraine has carried out a highly successful midrange strike campaign that has disrupted Russian logistics and supply lines, further slowing the Russian military’s advance. Kyiv has scaled up its long-range strike campaign, hitting military production facilities and civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia, including oil ports and refineries. Thanks to these attacks, about one-third of Russian oil-refining capacity is offline, causing gasoline shortages, fuel rationing, and long lines at the pumps that lasted from June until late July, and that will likely return when Ukraine restarts these strikes. In July, Ukraine started blowing up warehouses belonging to Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, making the war top of mind for ordinary consumers and affecting the thousands of Russian small and medium businesses that sell via the retail firm. Kyiv has also intensified efforts to isolate Crimea by targeting fuel supply routes and power generation facilities in the occupied peninsula. And Ukrainian drones are attacking Russian oil tankers and cargo vessels in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an attempt to stop the country’s maritime oil and grain exports.
Kyiv’s campaign is damaging Russia’s economy. The official 2026 forecast for Russian GDP growth is a meager 0.4 percent. Inflation is on the rise. To avoid even higher prices, the country’s central bank is keeping the interest rate at 14 percent. But this punishing figure makes credit prohibitively expensive for many businesses. Most worrying of all for the Kremlin, the budget deficit has swelled by $73 billion in the first six months of 2026, far exceeding the $48.5 billion it had anticipated for the entire year. Trump’s war against Iran has increased Russian oil revenues, but these inflows are not nearly enough to produce a cash cushion, and the monetary reserves Russia accumulated from decades of commodities exports, including from the war-induced commodities price boom in 2022, are gone. In order to finance its growing war bill, the Kremlin has to keep cutting nonmilitary expenditures and borrow domestically, right as Russian bond buyers are requesting higher risk premiums.
Thanks to these troubles, the Kremlin is losing support at home. The economic difficulties, energy blackouts, Internet restrictions, and general wartime fatigue have pushed Putin’s approval ratings from around 80 percent at the beginning of the year to 66 percent in mid-July. All available polling data indicates that the public mood in Russia is growing more uncertain and anxious. The country is becoming less and less convinced that its soldiers can win and that Putin has a realistic plan.
Given all these failures, Western governments might think that Putin would be willing to consider a meaningful settlement. But sadly, there is little to suggest this is the case. In fact, in all his recent public appearances, Putin has indicated that his war aims haven’t changed at all. “Unable to defeat Russia on the battlefield, our adversaries are resorting to outright terrorist methods against our people,” he declared on July 27. “But the people of Russia can never be broken.”
Unfortunately, Putin still has the power to back up such statements. The Russian economy may be struggling, but it is not on the verge of collapse. Moscow can keep paying for the war by forcing businesses to absorb the cost of drone attacks rather than spending on better drone defenses or compensating damaged firms. It can make regional governments absorb rising defense costs via smaller budgets, and it can compel households to absorb war costs in the form of higher inflation. The Kremlin can cut more civilian expenditures from the national budget, too. Right now, Russia is spending eight percent of its GDP on defense—a high figure—but far less than what the Soviet Union or the United States spent during World War II, or the nearly 40 percent Ukraine is spending right now.
These policies will make Russians angrier and poorer. But the Kremlin is insulated from mounting dissatisfaction. The regime has sophisticated tools of repression, including blanket censorship laws, AI-powered surveillance tools, and expanded law enforcement agencies, that can contain any outbursts. Public frustration with the economy might also be offset by a growing rally-around-the-flag effect. As Ukrainian attacks intensify and affect more people, ordinary Russians may well conclude that the war against Kyiv is a war for national survival, just as Putin has long suggested. Polling by the independent Levada Center shows that support for the actions of the Russian armed forces sits above 65 percent nationwide, with less than 25 percent of the population opposed.
